The High-End Neighborhoods Engineering Their Own Waves
 
Plus, Prague’s red-hot real-estate market and an Ottawa Tudor’s $1.2 million renovation
 
By Kerry Barger
 
 
Asa Cascavilla during a surf session at Waco Surf. Homes will cost between $99,000 for a townhouse to $3.3 million for a five-bedroom house. ANDY JACOBSOHN FOR WSJ
 

This is an edition of the WSJ Homes newsletter, a weekly guide to luxurious properties, celebrity homes, interior design and the housing market. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here.

 

Picture catching the perfect wave—minus the sharks, jellyfish, rocks, and bad currents. While those hazards usually come with the territory of surfing, developers in states like Texas, Utah, and Arizona are rewriting the rules by building communities around artificial lagoons.

 

Instead of golf courses, ski mountains or lakes, these developments—often with custom-built homes and members-only clubhouses—offer artificial waves at the main amenity. They not only mimic ocean waves but also allow more surfers per day, making building resorts around them more financially feasible.

 

“This kind of surfing is much more efficient,” said Asa Cascavilla, 50, a real-estate developer based in Dallas. Cascavilla, who grew up surfing, is planning to spend $2.2 million building a five-bedroom home at the Desperado, an 88-unit residential community at artificial-wave lagoon Waco Surf.

 

Whether these capital-intensive projects can be financially successful, however, remains to be seen; at least one planned project has already faltered.

 
 
ANDY JACOBSOHN FOR WSJ
 

Four decades after the fall of Communist rule, Prague’s real-estate market is booming. Between 2021 and 2025, the city’s sale prices jumped 33%, with a 14.6% increase in 2025 alone, according to a Knight Frank wealth report. The country’s rapid price growth is being driven by its growing wealth, a shortage of inventory in sought-after neighborhoods and investors drawn by relatively affordable prices, local experts told us.

 

Finally, when two lawyers purchased a 1920s Tudor in Ottawa, they knew it needed work. But they ultimately spent $1.2 million redoing the home’s 17 rooms—nearly as much as they paid for the house itself.

 
 
 

The Surf Communities Selling Man-Made Waves to Homeowners

 
 
ANDY JACOBSOHN FOR WSJ
 

Developers in states like Texas, Utah, and Arizona are betting that man-made surf lagoons will lure wealthy buyers, despite high construction costs and steep monthly fees.

 
 
 
CONTENT FROM: WHITECAP
 
 
Whitecap: The New Watermark in Texas Coastal Living
 
The Texas Gulf Coast doesn't let go easily. At Whitecap, that pull becomes a place to put down roots. Now available on North Padre Island, a rare collection of homesites from the $300s unfolds across five miles of navigable canals, where private docks lead to open water and the landscape stretches into a 30-acre nature preserve.
 
Learn More  >
 
 
 

Buying a House in Prague Isn’t the Bargain It Once Was

 
 
MILAN JAROŠ FOR WSJ
 

A scarcity of homes for sale and rapidly rising property prices are pushing younger buyers outside the city center.

 
 
 

A $1.2 Million Renovation Rescued an Awkward, 17-Room Tudor From the ‘80s

 
 
KEITO NEWMAN FOR WSJ
 

An Ottawa couple fixed mismatched floors, a tavern-like library and a ‘hideous staircase’ to make their ‘Frankenhouse’ feel less disjointed.

 
 
 

What’s the Deal?

 
 
CHAD SALVADOR/WWD/GETTY IMAGES (PATTY SMYTH AND JOHN MCENROE); MIKE HELFRICH
 

Two big-ticket home deals in Palm Beach, Fla., have fallen apart in recent months, both involving former Trump adviser Alina Mildon and her husband, Turkish executive Turhan Mildon.

 

A $55 million compound with an underground bunker in the wealthy Arizona town of Paradise Valley is looking to break the state’s home-sale record of $40.2 million.

 

Amid a string of big-ticket sales on Nantucket, a historic home overlooking Nantucket Harbor has sold for $42.5 million, a record for the affluent island off the coast of Massachusetts.

 

Want to see more deals? Sign up for our Mansion Deals email alert to have the biggest and best luxury home sales and listings delivered to your inbox.

 
 
 

The Luxe Life

 
 
STEVE AND CLEON RANDON/RANDON STUDIO
 

In the French Quarter of New Orleans, a beer warehouse-turned-private residence is on the market for $7.1 million. If it sells at that price, it would set the record for the most expensive home sale in the city.

 

Daniel Radcliffe unexpectedly met the producer and screenwriter for “Harry Potter” during the intermission of a play. “The encounter’s randomness made my parents think the universe was involved and they shouldn’t hold me back.”

 
 
 

House of the Week

 
 
DONKIN MEDIA
 

WSJ’s House of the Week brings readers to Philadelphia, where a 19th-century brick row house is on the market for the first time in 30 years.

 

The owner first spotted it while working at Walnut Street Theatre in the 1970s. “I ogled it,” says Randy Swartz, who paid $450,000 for the townhome in 1996 and spent roughly $250,000 updating the interior, remodeling bathrooms and the primary suite.

 
 
 

Your Home

 

• Zillow reported a decline in traffic to its apps and sites in the midst of what it called “one of the toughest housing markets in a generation.”

 

• Churches across the U.S. are working with developers to build affordable housing on underused land to sustain ministries and ease shortages.

 

• The U.S. is in a desperate battle to lower the cost to build housing. It’s losing.
